item.title: Amravati sex scandal
item.description: The Amravati case involves allegations that minor girls were sexually exploited, their intimate activities were secretly recorded, and the recordings were circulated online. Police investigated an apartment in Amravati and seized several electronic devices. These devices became important evidence because investigators needed to find the original videos, deleted files, messages and other digital information. The case shows how sexual crimes can be connected with cybercrime and digital evidence.

item.title: Mysuru-Bengaluru Highway Cases
item.description: This case involved a fatal collision on the Mysuru–Bengaluru Highway in which a minor allegedly drove a car and lost control near Dandi Maramma Temple. The car crossed the road divider and struck a motorcycle carrying a family. Three family members died and one child was injured. Police documented the scene through a mahazar, seized the involved car and conducted post-mortem examinations. The case later developed into a criminal proceeding involving the minor's father, including a charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. In August 2026, the Karnataka High Court was considering the father's challenge to the Section 304 Part II charge, while the criminal trial remained pending.

item.title: Blue drum case
item.description: Saurabh Rajput returned home from sea duty to celebrate his wife's and daughter's birthdays. While home, his wife Muskan and her lover Sahil conspired to eliminate him. On March 3, after eating sedated food, Saurabh was killed and dismembered in his home. To obscure the timeline, the accused purchased a 250 kg capacity blue plastic drum and sacks of cement from local markets, sealed Saurabh's remains inside, and fled on a vacation trip to Himachal Pradesh using Saurabh's phone to post updates and deceive family members. Following growing suspicion and police questioning upon their return, Muskan eventually confessed to her parents and police, leading to the recovery of the drum.

item.title: The Satyam Computer Services scandal
item.description: Often referred to as “India’s Enron,” the 2009 Satyam Computer Services scandal stands as one of the most notorious corporate frauds in Indian history. The deception unraveled on January 7, 2009, when the company’s founder and chairman, Byrraju Ramalinga Raju, confessed to systematically manipulating financial records for years, inflating revenues, profits, and cash balances to make the Hyderabad-based IT giant appear robust. To sustain the illusion, management forged bank statements, created fake invoices, and even invented roughly 10,000 "ghost" employees to siphoning off salary funds into real estate investments. The fraud, estimated at over ₹7,000 crore, finally collapsed after investors revolted against a desperate, conflicted bid to acquire two Raju-linked companies Maytas Infrastructure and Maytas Properties to plug the financial deficit. Following extensive investigations by the CBI, SEBI, and SFIO, a special court on April 9, 2015, convicted Raju and nine others, sentencing them to seven years of rigorous imprisonment for criminal conspiracy and falsification of accounts. To preserve business continuity and protect over 40,000 jobs, the Indian government swiftly dissolved the compromised board and facilitated the acquisition of Satyam by Tech Mahindra, while simultaneously enacting historic regulatory overhauls through the Companies Act of 2013 to enforce mandatory auditor rotation, strengthen independent director oversight, and tighten corporate governance frameworks nationwide.

item.title: Tandoor murder case
item.description: The Tandoor Murder Case (1995) involved Naina Sahni, who was murdered by her husband Sushil Sharma due to suspicion of an affair. Sharma shot her and, with the help of Keshav Kumar, tried to destroy the evidence by burning her body in a tandoor. Forensic investigation, DNA profiling, ballistic examination, and a second autopsy proved that Naina had died from gunshot injuries before being burned. The case highlighted the importance of forensic science in criminal investigations and became one of India's most famous murder cases.

item.title: Citibank–MphasiS Call Center Fraud Case
item.description: The Citibank–MphasiS Call Center Fraud Case (2005) was one of India’s earliest major cybercrime cases. It occurred in Pune, where employees of the MphasiS call center misused confidential customer information of Citibank clients. Using social engineering and voice phishing techniques, they obtained customers’ PINs and transferred about US$300,000–350,000 into fake bank accounts in India. The fraud was discovered after customers reported unauthorized transactions. Police arrested several accused and collected digital evidence such as login records, transaction logs, and forged documents. The case became a landmark example of insider cybercrime, banking fraud, and digital forensic investigation in India.

item.title: Jessica murder
item.description: On the night of April 29–30, 1999, Indian model Jessica Lal was shot and killed while working as a celebrity barmaid at an unlicensed party in Mehrauli, Delhi, after refusing to serve alcohol past closing time to Manu Sharma, the son of a prominent politician. The subsequent police investigation faced severe hurdles, most notably when several key eyewitnesses turned hostile and the murder weapon went missing, forcing the prosecution to rely on circumstantial evidence and forensics. Due to these setbacks, a trial court initially acquitted Sharma in February 2006; however, intense public outrage and media pressure prompted an appeal in the Delhi High Court, which overturned the decision and sentenced him to life imprisonment later that year a verdict subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court. After serving nearly 17 years of his sentence in Tihar Jail, Manu Sharma was officially released in June 2020 on the grounds of good behavior.

item.title: R.G Kar Medical College Rape And Murder Case
item.description: A postgraduate trainee doctor was found dead in the seminar room at R.G. Kar Medical College and Hospital on 9th August 2024. Initially investigated by the Kolkata Police, the case was transferred to the Central Bureau of Investigation for trials. The crime scene investigation included examination of biological, DNA, and physical evidence, as well as digital evidence. As part of investigations, biological, DNA, hair, clothing, footwear, and bluetooth evidence were analyzed. In relation to digital evidence, CCTV footage, mobile phone data, and call detail record analysis were conducted. Finally, a chargesheet by the CBI against the accused, Sanjay Roy, resulted in his conviction and life imprisonment by the trial court in January 2025. Notably, this case is of significance to forensic science due to the aspects of the crime scene investigation, including presenting evidence to the court to ensure the offender’s conviction.

item.title: The Nithari Serial Murders
item.description: The Nithari Serial Murders were a series of disappearances and killings of children and young women that occurred between 2005 and 2006 in Nithari village, Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The case was exposed on 29 December 2006 when human skeletal remains were discovered near House D-5, leading to the arrest of Moninder Singh Pandher and his servant Surinder Koli. The investigation, later handled by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), alleged that Koli lured victims into the house, murdered them, and disposed of their bodies. Although both men were initially convicted and sentenced to death in several cases, higher courts later found major flaws in the investigation and evidence. In 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both accused, and in 2025 the Supreme Court of India overturned Koli’s last remaining conviction, leaving the case as a significant example of investigative and forensic failures in Indian criminal justice history.

item.title: The Sheena Bora Murder Case
item.description: The Sheena Bora murder case is a high-profile legal battle centered around identity deception, domestic conflict, and financial motives. To protect her status in elite society after marrying media tycoon Peter Mukerjea, Indrani Mukerjea hid that Sheena was her biological daughter, publicly presenting her as a younger sister. When Sheena became romantically involved with Peter's son, Rahul Mukerjea, Indrani vehemently opposed the relationship, driven by fears of social exposure and inheritance disputes. According to the CBI, on April 24, 2012, Indrani, her ex-husband Sanjeev Khanna, and driver Shyamvar Rai allegedly lured, sedated, and strangled Sheena in a rented car, later burning her remains in the Raigad district. Indrani covered up the crime for three years by sending fake emails and texts claiming Sheena had moved to the United States. The plot unraveled in August 2015 when the driver was arrested on an unrelated charge and confessed, leading to the arrests of all key suspects. Today, the trial is in its final stages in a special Mumbai court under a strict timeline to conclude, with all primary accused individuals currently out on bail

item.title: GEETA CHOPRA AND SANJAY CHOPRA DOUBLE MURDER KIDNAPPING CASS
item.description: The Geeta Chopra and Sanjay Chopra murder case, popularly known as the Ranga-Billa case, was one of the most notorious kidnapping and murder cases in India. It occurred in New Delhi on 26 August 1978 and involved the kidnapping and killing of siblings Geeta Chopra and Sanjay Chopra by Kuljeet Singh alias Ranga Khus and Jasbir Singh alias Billa. The kidnappers, Kuljeet Singh alias Ranga and Jasbir Singh alias Billa, abducted the children and later murdered them. Their bodies were recovered from the Delhi Ridge on 28 August 1978. Forensic and medical evidence, including injuries, fingerprints, and hospital records, played an important role in connecting the accused to the crime.
